pos: n. (proper name; a son of Hammoleketh, of the house of Manasseh)
etymology: Hebrew Ishhod, man of renown or man of majesty, from ish, a man, and hod, honour or majesty; named once, at 1 Chronicles 7:18.
biblical_def: Ishod is a son of Hammoleketh, in the genealogy of Manasseh, and he is named once: “And his sister Hammoleketh bare Ishod, and Abiezer, and Mahalah” (1 Chronicles 7:18). The lines around him are unusual in that the women are named and their standing noted. The chapter has already said of Manasseh's house: “The sons of Manasseh; Ashriel, whom she bare: ( but his concubine the Aramitess bare Machir the father of Gilead” (1 Chronicles 7:14); then the descent through Gilead is traced: “And the sons of Ulam; Bedan. These were the sons of Gilead, the son of Machir, the son of Manasseh” (1 Chronicles 7:17), and the next verse after Ishod names another family: “And the sons of Shemida were, Ahian, and Shechem, and Likhi, and Aniam” (1 Chronicles 7:19). Hammoleketh's own name means the queen or she who reigns, and she is named as the one who bore these sons, her brother's line being traced beside hers. Ishod's name means man of renown, and he has none: one mention, three brothers and sisters, and silence.

corruption_summary: A name is treated as a promise of greatness; a man called man of renown is mentioned once in all of Scripture.
corruption_paragraphs: Hebrew parents named their children with hope, and some of those children lived lives the names never came near. Ishod means man of renown; what is recorded of him is his mother's name and the names of two siblings. A high name is not a prophecy, and a quiet life is not a failure of one.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that honour belongs to God to bestow, that a godly mother's household is recorded in Scripture by her own name, and that most of God's people live and die unrenowned.

pos: n. (proper name; a son of Beriah, of the tribe of Benjamin)
etymology: Hebrew Yishpah, perhaps he will be bald or bare, of uncertain derivation; named once, at 1 Chronicles 8:16.
biblical_def: Ispah is one of the sons of Beriah in the long Benjamite genealogy of First Chronicles eight, and he is named once: “And Michael, and Ispah, and Joha, the sons of Beriah” (1 Chronicles 8:16). The families around him fill the same bare pattern: “And Ahio, Shashak, and Jeremoth” (1 Chronicles 8:14); “And Zebadiah, and Arad, and Ader” (1 Chronicles 8:15); and after him “And Zebadiah, and Meshullam, and Hezeki, and Heber” (1 Chronicles 8:17). This chapter exists for a particular purpose. Benjamin was nearly destroyed in the days of the judges, and Benjamin gave Israel its first king, and Benjamin returned from Babylon with Judah when the northern tribes did not. So the Chronicler, writing for a people rebuilding after the exile, spends a whole chapter proving that the tribe of Saul and of Mordecai and of Paul still had its houses and their names. Ispah's single mention is a brick in that wall.

corruption_summary: Chronicles' lists are called padding; the Benjamite genealogy proves a nearly destroyed tribe still had its houses.
corruption_paragraphs: A reader who meets four verses of names asks what they are for. Benjamin had been cut down to six hundred men in the days of the judges, and the Chronicler is writing to a remnant that had just come out of captivity. A full roll of Benjamite houses told that remnant that God had not let the tribe die, and that His promises were not a matter of sentiment but of names.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God preserves what He has promised to preserve, and that He does it household by household, with the names kept.

pos: n. (proper name; a chief of the Gadites in Bashan)
etymology: Hebrew Ya'nay, perhaps whom the LORD answers, from anah, to answer; named once, at 1 Chronicles 5:12.
biblical_def: Jaanai is one of the chiefs of Gad on the east of Jordan. The Chronicler sets the tribe in its place first: “And the children of Gad dwelt over against them, in the land of Bashan unto Salchah” (1 Chronicles 5:11), and then names the leading men: “Joel the chief, and Shapham the next, and Jaanai, and Shaphat in Bashan” (1 Chronicles 5:12). Their brethren follow: “And their brethren of the house of their fathers were, Michael, and Meshullam, and Sheba, and Jorai, and Jachan, and Zia, and Heber, seven” (1 Chronicles 5:13). The eastern tribes were a fighting people, and the Chronicler gives their muster: “The sons of Reuben, and the Gadites, and half the tribe of Manasseh, of valiant men, men able to bear buckler and sword, and to shoot with bow, and skilful in war, were four and forty thousand seven hundred and threescore, that went out to the war” (1 Chronicles 5:18). These were the tribes that chose land outside the Jordan for the sake of their cattle, and they were the first to be carried away captive. The pastures were good and the border was exposed.

corruption_summary: Good pasture is mistaken for God's provision; the tribes who settled outside Jordan for their cattle were taken captive first.
corruption_paragraphs: Reuben, Gad and half Manasseh asked for the land east of Jordan because it suited their herds, and Moses granted it on terms. They were skilful in war and well supplied, and they were also outside the line God had drawn and first in the path of Assyria. A choice made for the flocks is not thereby a choice made in faith.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that prosperity is not evidence of a right decision, and that God's people are safest within the bounds He has set for them.

pos: n. (proper name; one of the sons of Bani who put away a strange wife under Ezra)
etymology: Hebrew Ya'asu, perhaps they will do or maker, from asah, to do or make; named once, at Ezra 10:37.
biblical_def: Jaasau is one of the men named in Ezra's register of those who had married foreign wives and were brought to put them away: “Mattaniah, Mattenai, and Jaasau” (Ezra 10:37). The names run on without comment on either side: “Vaniah, Meremoth, Eliashib” (Ezra 10:36), and “And Bani, and Binnui, Shimei” (Ezra 10:38). Then the chapter closes with its one sentence of summary and weight: “All these had taken strange wives: and some of them had wives by whom they had children” (Ezra 10:44). It is a hard chapter and Scripture does not make it easy. The sin was not that these women were foreign by blood — Ruth was a Moabitess and is in the line of Christ — but that they were of the peoples whose idolatry had already destroyed the kingdom once, taken into the households of a nation newly returned from the judgment that idolatry brought. The remnant was small enough that a generation of such marriages would have ended it.

corruption_summary: Ezra's reform is charged with racial prejudice; the issue was the idolatry of the peoples of the land, not their blood.
corruption_paragraphs: The tenth chapter of Ezra is regularly read as a piece of ethnic cleansing, and the charge misses what the same Scriptures say elsewhere. Rahab the Canaanite and Ruth the Moabitess were received, married into Israel, and placed in the genealogy of Christ. What Ezra confronted was marriage into the idolatrous households of the land by a remnant that had just been destroyed for idolatry.

The remnant was a few thousand people. A generation of households where the mother worshipped the gods of the land would have finished what Nebuchadnezzar began. The reform was severe because the danger was total, and the men who submitted to it are named.

pos: n. (proper name; a son of Tola, of the tribe of Issachar)
etymology: Hebrew Yachmay, perhaps whom the LORD guards or warm, of uncertain derivation; named once, at 1 Chronicles 7:2.
biblical_def: Jahmai is a son of Tola in the genealogy of Issachar. The tribe is set out at the head of the chapter: “Now the sons of Issachar were, Tola, and Puah, Jashub, and Shimron, four” (1 Chronicles 7:1), and Tola's sons are then named with a notice of what they were: “And the sons of Tola; Uzzi, and Rephaiah, and Jeriel, and Jahmai, and Jibsam, and Shemuel, heads of their father's house, to wit, of Tola: they were valiant men of might in their generations; whose number was in the days of David two and twenty thousand and six hundred” (1 Chronicles 7:2). The next generation is given too: “And the sons of Uzzi; Izrahiah: and the sons of Izrahiah; Michael, and Obadiah, and Joel, Ishiah, five: all of them chief men” (1 Chronicles 7:3), and the tribal muster follows: “And their brethren among all the families of Issachar were valiant men of might, reckoned in all by their genealogies fourscore and seven thousand” (1 Chronicles 7:5). Issachar is the tribe of whom it was said that its men had understanding of the times and knew what Israel ought to do. Jahmai is one of the heads of that house.

corruption_summary: Spiritual and civil strength are set against each other; the heads of Issachar's houses are called valiant men of might and men who knew the times.
corruption_paragraphs: It is assumed that a man of discernment is not a man of action, and that a fighter does not understand his age. Issachar was the tribe credited with understanding of the times, and the Chronicler calls the heads of its houses valiant men of might and gives their muster. The two went together in the same families.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that godly men are to have both understanding of the times and the courage to act in them, and that the heads of households are responsible for both.

pos: n. (proper name; a prince of Simeon in the days of Hezekiah)
etymology: Hebrew Yamlek, he shall make king or may he cause to reign, from malak, to reign; named once, at 1 Chronicles 4:34.
biblical_def: Jamlech is one of the princes of Simeon whose names the Chronicler records in connection with a conquest in the reign of Hezekiah. The place is set first: “And all their villages that were round about the same cities, unto Baal. These were their habitations, and their genealogy” (1 Chronicles 4:33); then the men: “And Meshobab, and Jamlech, and Joshah the son of Amaziah” (1 Chronicles 4:34). The Chronicler is explicit about their standing and their increase: “These mentioned by their names were princes in their families: and the house of their fathers increased greatly” (1 Chronicles 4:38). And then he tells what they did: “And these written by name came in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah, and smote their tents, and the habitations that were found there, and destroyed them utterly unto this day, and dwelt in their rooms: because there was pasture there for their flocks” (1 Chronicles 4:41). Simeon had been a tribe without a settled portion of its own, scattered in Judah's territory, and in a good reign its princes went out and took pasture. His name means he shall make king, and he served under a king who did right in the sight of the LORD.

corruption_summary: A tribe's scattered inheritance is read as a curse only; under a good king the princes of Simeon increased greatly and found pasture.
corruption_paragraphs: Jacob's word over Simeon was a word of division and scattering, and Simeon never held a separate territory. Yet in Hezekiah's reign the Chronicler records that the house of their fathers increased greatly and that their princes went out and took the pasture they needed. A judgment on a tribe did not shut the hand of God against it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God blesses His people under godly rule, that He remembers a scattered tribe, and that He records by name the men who acted in faith in a good reign.

pos: n. (proper name; a chief of the sons of Zerah who dwelt in Jerusalem)
etymology: Hebrew Ye'u'el, perhaps carried away of God or God has gathered; named once, at 1 Chronicles 9:6.
biblical_def: Jeuel is a chief of the house of Zerah, named among those who settled in Jerusalem after the captivity: “And of the sons of Zerah; Jeuel, and their brethren, six hundred and ninety” (1 Chronicles 9:6). The chapter sets out who came back to live in the holy city: “And in Jerusalem dwelt of the children of Judah, and of the children of Benjamin, and of the children of Ephraim, and Manasseh” (1 Chronicles 9:3). The numbers are given house by house: “And their brethren, according to their generations, nine hundred and fifty and six. All these men were chief of the fathers in the house of their fathers” (1 Chronicles 9:9), and of the priests it says something a reader ought not to pass by: “And their brethren, heads of the house of their fathers, a thousand and seven hundred and threescore; very able men for the work of the service of the house of God” (1 Chronicles 9:13). Very able men for the work of the service — that is how the Holy Ghost describes the workforce of the restored temple. Jeuel brought six hundred and ninety men of his house back to a ruined city.

corruption_paragraphs: We praise capability in the abstract and let a man choose what to spend it on. Scripture ties the two together: these were very able men, and they were able for the work of the service of the house of God. Their competence had an object, and the object was worship.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that gifts are given for the service of God's house, and that whole households willingly resettled a ruined city in order to serve there.

pos: n. (proper name; a son of Shaharaim by Hodesh, of the tribe of Benjamin)
etymology: Hebrew Ye'uts, perhaps counsellor, from uts, to take counsel; named once, at 1 Chronicles 8:10.
biblical_def: Jeuz is a son of Shaharaim, born in Moab after a domestic wreck that the Chronicler records without comment: “And Shaharaim begat children in the country of Moab, after he had sent them away; Hushim and Baara were his wives” (1 Chronicles 8:8). He put away two wives and took a third: “And he begat of Hodesh his wife, Jobab, and Zibia, and Mesha, and Malcham” (1 Chronicles 8:9), and the list of that household continues: “And Jeuz, and Shachia, and Mirma. These were his sons, heads of the fathers” (1 Chronicles 8:10). Then the earlier wife's children are named too: “And of Hushim he begat Abitub, and Elpaal” (1 Chronicles 8:11). It is a bleak little paragraph — a Benjamite in the land of Moab, dismissed wives, a second family, and sons who became heads of fathers' houses in Israel notwithstanding. The Holy Ghost does not pause to moralize. He writes the facts and lets the reader see what polygamy and divorce look like when they are set down in a register.

Scripture narrates sin in the houses of its own people and leaves the law of God standing over it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the name. The principle to recover is that the Bible's honesty about the households of Israel is not approval, and that God may still raise heads of fathers' houses out of a broken home.

pos: n. (proper name; a son of Tola, of the tribe of Issachar)
etymology: Hebrew Yibsam, fragrant or pleasant, from basam, spice or balsam; named once, at 1 Chronicles 7:2.
biblical_def: Jibsam is a son of Tola in the genealogy of Issachar, and his name means fragrant. The tribe heads the chapter: “Now the sons of Issachar were, Tola, and Puah, Jashub, and Shimron, four” (1 Chronicles 7:1), and his own verse names him among his brothers with a word about their quality: “And the sons of Tola; Uzzi, and Rephaiah, and Jeriel, and Jahmai, and Jibsam, and Shemuel, heads of their father's house, to wit, of Tola: they were valiant men of might in their generations; whose number was in the days of David two and twenty thousand and six hundred” (1 Chronicles 7:2). The next generation is given: “And the sons of Uzzi; Izrahiah: and the sons of Izrahiah; Michael, and Obadiah, and Joel, Ishiah, five: all of them chief men” (1 Chronicles 7:3), and then the tribal total: “And their brethren among all the families of Issachar were valiant men of might, reckoned in all by their genealogies fourscore and seven thousand” (1 Chronicles 7:5). The phrase in their generations is worth weighing. The Chronicler does not say they were valiant once; he says that in their generations, each in his own time, they were men of might.

corruption_summary: Faithfulness is expected to be inherited automatically; the Chronicler says these men were valiant in their generations, each in his own time.
corruption_paragraphs: A godly family is thought to carry its children along by momentum, and children of such families often assume it. The text gives a different account: these were heads of their father's house, valiant men of might in their generations — which is to say that each generation had to be valiant in its own.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that every generation must stand on its own before God, and that an inheritance of faith is a trust to be exercised, not a possession to be enjoyed.

etymology: Hebrew Pispah, perhaps expansion or disappearance, of uncertain derivation; named once, at 1 Chronicles 7:38.
biblical_def: Pispah is a son of Jether in the genealogy of Asher, named once: “And the sons of Jether; Jephunneh, and Pispah, and Ara” (1 Chronicles 7:38). The verses around him list the other houses of the tribe: “Bezer, and Hod, and Shamma, and Shilshah, and Ithran, and Beera” (1 Chronicles 7:37), and “And the sons of Ulla; Arah, and Haniel, and Rezia” (1 Chronicles 7:39). The summary that closes the tribe is one of the warmest in the whole genealogy: “All these were the children of Asher, heads of their father's house, choice and mighty men of valour, chief of the princes. And the number throughout the genealogy of them that were apt to the war and to battle was twenty and six thousand men” (1 Chronicles 7:40). Asher was a northern tribe that never figures largely in the history, took little part in the great battles, and produced no judge and no king. The Chronicler calls its heads choice and mighty men of valour, chief of the princes, and counts twenty-six thousand of them fit for war.

corruption_summary: A people with no famous history is judged to have none worth keeping; God calls Asher's heads choice and mighty men of valour.
corruption_paragraphs: Asher gave Israel no judge, no king and no prophet, and appears in the narrative chiefly by not appearing. God's own summary of the tribe calls its heads choice and mighty men of valour, chief of the princes, and gives the number apt for war. His estimate of a people is not drawn from their press.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God values His people by what they are before Him, not by what the history remembers, and that quiet tribes have honourable men.
